I was limited in the use of the macro lense by having plants and other obstacles between this tiny weird creature and me. Pardosa xerampelina: The spider I have decided to report on is Pardosa xerampelina in the Lycosidae family. The Lycosidae family, more commonly known as the wolf spiders, are hunters. They scavenge during the day and hide in small crevices (under stones, rotten logs, etc.) at night. They can run fast, jump short distances, and they have very strong chelicera that they use to crush and eat the 5 to 15 small insects they consume each day.
Out of all the spiders, an interesting and very specific characteristic of the Lycosidae family is its mating practices and egg production. Because of the Lycosidae’s family trait of amazing vision, there is a very visual mating dance performed by the male to entice the female. The eggs, when produced, are placed in a silk sack that the female spins. Also, leg size is a morphological trait that really distinguishes the species from one another. All Lycosid’s have legs that are scopulate and spinose, but the genus Pardosa, have legs that are relatively long, with the metatarsi and tarsi quite thin and with very long spines. 
To begin my comparisons with the other Lycosidae specimens I collected, I will start by discussing the traits of the Pardosa genus. The Pardosa are classified as the ‘thin-legged’ wolf spiders. They are recognizable by their relatively long, spinose legs, and the high cephalothorax head region. Another defining characteristic is their smaller chelicerae. Their ground color is generally gray to black, although sometimes they can be more brown/tan or yellow. In the smaller Pardosa species, size is around 3.8-4 mm where in the upper sizes it can be somewhere close to 9-9.3 mm. When looking at my three collections in the Pardosa family, you can see the overall brownish coloring, the not-so-distinct lighter areas on the carapace, and the slightly more yellow spots on the abdomen. They measured 9mm, 9mm, and 8mm; all in the approximate size range for Pardosa xerampelina. My second genus, Trochosa, has the more distinct yellow coloration and the defining submarginal stripe on each side of the carapace. They also have a shorter and wider face then the Pardosa. My final genus is Tigrosa. This genus has clearly defined medial stripe and an abdomen with a broader light stripe. Its underside is normally solid black, but it can be spotted with lighter patches. 
The reproductive patterns of Pardosa xerampelina are include the location of a female by pheromones. Stopping a short distance away from her, the male will raise and lower his palps and legs, signaling his courtship display. With a satisfactory display, she will permit mating; the male places his swollen palpus inside the female and release sperm. After they mate, the female will most likely kill the male. 
The habitats of this species include woodland, shrub-land, forest, meadows, gardens, and homes. I found my xerampelina three of these described areas: the eves of my front porch, crawling across the road in woodland area, and among large rocks in our landscaping. 
When studying these spiders, I noticed that most of the variation came through the coloration. The tint of brown, tan, and yellows along the described patterns varied between the three identified Pardosa xerampelina. Another variation was the habitat of these species. I found each spider in a completely different environment. Thus, the food sources and habitat differentiated. The habitat of all Lycosidae is similar, but there were some major variations between the habitat of the Pardosa, Tigrosa and Trochosa genera. One of the main adaptations among the Lycosidae family is the legs. The Pardosa genus has adapted to have longer, skinnier legs that allow them to move with increased speed over their more common mountainous habitat. The Tigrosa and Trochosa genera have noticeably thicker legs, and although they too live in rougher areas, they do not have the speed the Pardosa do. A similarity between them was the main body coloration. All five Lycosidae spiders were a dark brown color. The other similarity was the darkness of their eyes. Wolf spiders are known for how dark their eyes are, compared to the lighter, glossier eyes of other arachnids. There are many variations in the species I looked at but this can be attributed to the fact that they are all in the same family.

Datos de Yopal: registrado en Bosque Seco Tropical (temporada de lluvia). Precipitación mínima de 15 – 25 mm en los meses de enero y diciembre, precipitación máxima 350 mm y 300 mm en los meses de mayo, junio y julio; con menos de 60 mm de lluvia en el mes más seco y precipitación anual superior a 1270 mm. Cuenta con valores mínimos de humedad relativa a inicio del año (65%), y valores más altos en junio, julio, agosto y septiembre (90-85%). Cuenta con una altura sobre el nivel del mar entre 0 y 1000 m, una pluviosidad entre 2000 y 4000 mm y temperatura promedio mayor de 24 °C, con amplitud de temperatura máxima de 8 °C, como se referencia en DANE. Los máximos valores de temperatura no sobrepasan los 36 °C y los mínimos valores no logran bajar los 19 °C que se presentan en febrero y en julio, respectivamente. Temperatura media anual mayor de 20 °C, con una estación seca y una lluviosa bien definidas (Bustamante et al., 2017; DANE, 1999; Castro y Sosa, 2017).

Se observa con frecuencia plantas representativas de la zona como Yarumo (Cecropia peltata), Jobo (Spondias mombin), Cedro (Cedrela odorata), Nauno (Albizzia guachepele), Cañafistol (Cassia moschata), Flor blanco (Tabebuia orinocensis), Uña de gato (Cynodon dactylon), entre otras.

Te dejo algunas recomendaciones para tus registros. Las fotografías y descripciones que hagas, te van a permitir identificar el ejemplar: más detalles ver: https://colombia.inaturalist.org/journal/teodoro_chivatabedoya/54937-registro-de-hongos-macromicetos

-Tomar fotografías de las diferentes estructuras del basidioma/ascoma/cuerpo fructifero/carpoforo/seta (por encima, por debajo y de perfil), su estipe (píe), píleo (sombrero) y base. En el caso de retirar el ejemplar sin conocerlo, debes comprometerte a realizar una descripción detallada para aportar a su conocimiento y que no quede en una muestra arrancada, fotografiada y desechada. Para trabajos de identificación, es necesario que retires el ejemplar completo, sin cortar o maltratar la base del estípite, de igual forma, tomar nota del tipo de sustrato (material donde crece y desarrolla).

-Es importante que describas las dimensiones (altura y diámetro), forma, consistencia, textura, color y olor. Recuerda que los ejemplares cambian bastante según su estado de desarrollo, así que es ideal familiarizarse con la zona y temporada en la que crecen, para hacer un seguimiento y logres observar la variabilidad fenotípica del basidioma o ascoma (cuerpo fructífero).

-Toma fotos del entorno y agrega datos del ecosistema (humedad, temperatura, altura, tipo de bosque, insectos asociados, etc).

-No olvides que la determinación de macromicetos es compleja y no se realiza únicamente con fotografías, esta tarea (a nivel de género y especie; en la mayoría) implica actividades de descripción morfológica externa e interna, esporada, reacciones químicas, microscopia e incluso herramientas moleculares (ADN/PCR).

description: Undescribed Scea sp. The little town of Aguas Calientes below Machu Picchu has a Machu Picchu Pueblo sign in 3-foot-high letters that's all lit up at night like the Great White Way. I found a couple of moths fluttering around its base the next morning. This bug led me on a merry chase -- both while photographing it and while trying to ID it. A google image search on "Arctiidae Machu Picchu" (sic; it turns out to be in the Notodontidae) turned up an exact match on the first page: tolweb.org/Scea_erasa/138757. But not so fast! That page, dated 2010 and written by lepidopterists Jim Miller and Andrew Brower, describes Scea erasa, but notes that it is "A rare species ... mostly from the slopes of the Andes in Junín and San Martín provinces .... Very similar to Scea bryki and an undescribed species from Machu Picchu." Scea bryki is even rarer, and likewise from the wrong area. Jim Miller kindly confirmed to me by email that yes, this appears to be his undescribed Scea sp. from Machu Picchu, and no, he hasn't published it yet.

Recomendaciones para su registro, descripción y posterior determinación:
-Fotografiar estructuras del basidioma/cuerpo fructifero/carpoforo/seta (por encima, por debajo y de perfil), en el caso de retirar el ejemplar sin conocerlo, debes comprometerte a realizar una descripción detallada para aportar a su conocimiento y que no quede en una muestra arrancada, fotografiada y desechada.
-Es importante que describas las dimensiones, forma, consistencia, textura, color y olor. Recuerda que los ejemplares cambian bastante según su estado de desarrollo, así que es ideal familiarizarse con la zona (sustrato) para hacer un seguimiento y logres detallar la variabilidad fenotípica del basidioma o ascoma (cuerpo fructífero)
-Toma fotos del entorno y agrega datos del ecosistema (humedad, temperatura, altura y tipo de bosque).
-No olvides que la determinación de hongos es compleja y no se realiza únicamente con fotografías, esta tarea (a nivel de genero y especie; en la mayoría) implica otras actividades como descripción morfológica externa e interna, reacciones químicas, microscopia y ADN.

Species Name: Oak-loving Elfin Saddle

Kingdom: Fungi

Shape: Saddle-shaped caps of Helvella lacunosa often have three or more contorted lobes. The cap edges join to the stem to form a multi-lobed inner chamber with several openings.

Size: Typically 2 to 4cm across the cap, Elfin Saddle fungi have a total height 4 to 10cm.

Coloration: The smooth outer surface of the cap is dark grey and is the surface that bears the spores, while the infertile inner surface is also grey but has a felty feel. Longitudinally grooved and hollow, the stems are grey or grey-brown and often contain many inner chambers.

Characteristic: They have microscopic flask-shaped structures on the fertile cap surface that produce spores.

Reference: 

https://www.first-nature.com/fungi/helvella-lacunosa.php

Location: USF Riverfront Park, Tampa, FL, US

Habitat: This species seems to favor rich soil and burnt ground, against which as a background it is not at all conspicuous and so is easily missed. 

Distribution: A fairly common find in Britain and Ireland, Elfin Saddle fungus occurs also throughout mainland Europe, from Scandinavia right down to the southern shores of the Iberian Peninsula. This species is also found in North America

description:
Recomendaciones para su registro, descripción y posterior determinación:
-Fotografiar estructuras del basidioma/cuerpo fructifero/carpoforo/seta (por encima, por debajo y de perfil), en el caso de retirar el ejemplar sin conocerlo, debes comprometerte a realizar una descripción detallada para aportar a su conocimiento y que no quede en una muestra arrancada, fotografiada y desechada.
-Es importante que describas las dimensiones, forma, consistencia, textura, color y olor. Recuerda que los ejemplares cambian bastante según su estado de desarrollo, así que es ideal familiarizarse con la zona (sustrato) para hacer un seguimiento y logres detallar la variabilidad fenotípica del basidioma o ascoma (cuerpo fructífero)
-Toma fotos del entorno y agrega datos del ecosistema (humedad, temperatura, altura, tipo de bosque, etc).
-No olvides que la determinación de hongos es compleja y no se realiza únicamente con fotografías, esta tarea (a nivel de genero y especie; en la mayoría) implica otras actividades como descripción morfológica externa e interna, reacciones químicas, microscopia y ADN.

Recomendaciones para su registro, descripción y posterior determinación:
-Fotografiar estructuras del basidioma/cuerpo fructifero/carpoforo/seta (por encima, por debajo y de perfil), en el caso de retirar el ejemplar sin conocerlo, debes comprometerte a realizar una descripción detallada para aportar a su conocimiento y que no quede en una muestra arrancada, fotografiada y desechada.
-Es importante que describas las dimensiones, forma, consistencia, textura, color y olor. Recuerda que los ejemplares cambian bastante según su estado de desarrollo, así que es ideal familiarizarse con la zona (sustrato) para hacer un seguimiento y logres detallar la variabilidad fenotípica del basidioma o ascoma (cuerpo fructífero)
-Toma fotos del entorno y agrega datos del ecosistema (humedad, temperatura, altura, tipo de bosque, etc).
-No olvides que la determinación de hongos es compleja y no se realiza únicamente con fotografías, esta tarea (a nivel de genero y especie; en la mayoría) implica otras actividades como descripción morfológica externa e interna, reacciones químicas, microscopia y ADN.

description:
This observation is the earwig. The eggs are in a separate observation. If you happen to know if the eggs are from the earwig, I’d love to know.

The earwigs were half to three quarters of an inch long. They were very shiny and metallic looking, but not just the silvery metals. They had highlights of steel blue, coppery red, dark green, and bright blue. 

 I found them after I moved a bag of mulch that was laid on an existing mulched bed. The newly exposed, tiny, bright white spheres caught my eye so I checked them out. There was an insect lying nearby not moving as I tried to focus on the itsy bitty eggs with my phone and clip-on macro lens. The insect then started removing one egg at a time from the pile and carrying it down into the old mulch through little tunnels. A second insect came up and helped. A third earwig came over, pulled an egg out of the pile and then left without the egg. They had moved about half of the eggs down below before it got to dark to see. 

The eggs have their own observation, so I can annotate the life two stages: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/42302583

description:
These mushrooms were found in San Ramon, California in a grassy area off a trail on May 3rd, 2020. The identification of these mushrooms is Tricholoma Murrillianum.  

The observed behavior of these mushrooms was that they grew all next to each other not very spread out and were in a shaded area beneath a tree with grass and other a few other plants surrounding. Tricholoma Murrillianum has a few unique markings on top and has white-ish rounded tops. I found it while walking on the trail and was excited to find some bigger mushrooms. I like how rounded the tops are and they remind me of what I picture in my head when someone says mushrooms. 
After doing some research, I found that they are in fact edible and humans can eat Tricholoma Murrillianum. They are firm with good flavor, have a spicy odor, and have a meaty texture.

description:
EUCALYPT FOREST

Observations were taken on 6 Sep 2020, almost a year after the site was burnt.

Observations at this site at Binna Burra were taken between the picnic area and the former lodge. It is an area of sclerophyll forest, a vegetation type representative of a relatively small part of Lamington National Park (most of which is rainforest).

After a long dry period, on 8 Sep 2019 the Sarabah fire swept up the slopes of the Lamington Plateau, pushed by strong wind from the west. This major fire burnt in the district for some days before and after this date. Much of the eucalypt forest along the ridge between Binna Burra and the village of Beechmont was burnt, illustrating the scale of, and danger posed by, this blaze. 

Binna Burra was evacuated in a timely manner and the sole access road closed. After the fire front had passed, surveys by helicopter confirmed that the historic Rainforest Lodge, on the hilltop, had been destroyed. Other major private and QPWS structures of the area remained largely in-tact. 
At the time of these observations (Sep 2020) the site of the lodge had been cleared, and dangerous trees felled or branches lopped. Most park facilities and other accommodations have reopened with repairs to the access road completed by 1 Sep 2020. 

Many mature eucalypts showed trunk and branch resprouting, while newly shooting native plants and weeds were seen alongside the road between the picnic area and the former lodge.

Datos de Yopal: registrado en Bosque Seco Tropical (temporada de lluvia). Precipitación mínima de 15 – 25 mm en los meses de enero y diciembre, precipitación máxima 350 mm y 300 mm en los meses de mayo, junio y julio; con menos de 60 mm de lluvia en el mes más seco y precipitación anual superior a 1270 mm. Cuenta con valores mínimos de humedad relativa a inicio del año (65%), y valores más altos en junio, julio, agosto y septiembre (90-85%). Cuenta con una altura sobre el nivel del mar entre 0 y 1000 m, una pluviosidad entre 2000 y 4000 mm y temperatura promedio mayor de 24 °C, con amplitud de temperatura máxima de 8 °C, como se referencia en DANE. Los máximos valores de temperatura no sobrepasan los 36 °C y los mínimos valores no logran bajar los 19 °C que se presentan en febrero y en julio, respectivamente. Temperatura media anual mayor de 20 °C, con una estación seca y una lluviosa bien definidas (Bustamante et al., 2017; DANE, 1999; Castro y Sosa, 2017).

Se observa con frecuencia plantas representativas de la zona como Yarumo (Cecropia peltata), Jobo (Spondias mombin), Cedro (Cedrela odorata), Nauno (Albizzia guachepele), Cañafistol (Cassia moschata), Flor blanco (Tabebuia orinocensis), Uña de gato (Cynodon dactylon), entre otras.

Te dejo algunas recomendaciones para tus registros. Las fotografías y descripciones que hagas, te van a permitir identificar el ejemplar: más detalles ver: https://colombia.inaturalist.org/journal/teodoro_chivatabedoya/54937-registro-de-hongos-macromicetos

-Tomar fotografías de las diferentes estructuras del basidioma/ascoma/cuerpo fructifero/carpoforo/seta (por encima, por debajo y de perfil), su estipe (píe), píleo (sombrero) y base. En el caso de retirar el ejemplar sin conocerlo, debes comprometerte a realizar una descripción detallada para aportar a su conocimiento y que no quede en una muestra arrancada, fotografiada y desechada. Para trabajos de identificación, es necesario que retires el ejemplar completo, sin cortar o maltratar la base del estípite, de igual forma, tomar nota del tipo de sustrato (material donde crece y desarrolla).

-Es importante que describas las dimensiones (altura y diámetro), forma, consistencia, textura, color y olor. Recuerda que los ejemplares cambian bastante según su estado de desarrollo, así que es ideal familiarizarse con la zona y temporada en la que crecen, para hacer un seguimiento y logres observar la variabilidad fenotípica del basidioma o ascoma (cuerpo fructífero).

-Toma fotos del entorno y agrega datos del ecosistema (humedad, temperatura, altura, tipo de bosque, insectos asociados, etc).

-No olvides que la determinación de macromicetos es compleja y no se realiza únicamente con fotografías, esta tarea (a nivel de género y especie; en la mayoría) implica actividades de descripción morfológica externa e interna, esporada, reacciones químicas, microscopia e incluso herramientas moleculares (ADN/PCR).

description:
I was taking my dogs to the vet and thought initially this was some scat, after further "digging" into it I understood that it was a mushroom. Found growing outside of the clinic under two cultivated hardwood trees. My impression was that it could be a Lactarius species, but I was left speechless after what happened next. 

The first specimen I tried to pull out ended up in failure as I snapped the base off which left a majority of the fruit body in the ground. I thought this was odd, so for the next specimen I carefully dug around the base to find a massive sclerotia of mycelium! The sclerotia was about the same size as the stipe, which was unique to me as well (somewhat bulbous, short and stubbed). A couple of the photos (I think #2-3) were taken 30 seconds after holding the sclerotia under water, attempting to wash away the dirt and debris. 

The cross section of the specimen shows that it has an empty "pith" in the stipe, or is somewhat hollow as you can see. The sclerotia is just a hardened ball of dirt and mycelium, literally feels like a rock now. 

Usually I can put a genus to most of the fungi I see, but this one is different. Eventually I will update with additional information and photos of spores. I wish I would have taken better photos but my dogs were getting antsy.

description:
The Story
I was walking around through the forest when I noticed what appeared to be blood on a stick. For about ~100 meters of land there was the same blood looking stuff on several sticks, rocks, a stump and across a log. My thinking was that either a raptor had a meal at these locations or a bob cat, or a mountain lion was dragging its kill. I also considered it was a wounded deer or bear. I even brought a sample stick home with me if I found someone to possible DNA test it. I saw this same thing in another location near here and once in another area of the basin about 6 miles away as if a wounded animal blood trail.
Fast forward 2 years and I came across this observation of porcupine urine.
https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/2657215
Suddenly I thought, "Maybe what I saw was the same thing!"
So I then spent the next 2 days trying to locate the pictures I took. I finally located them on an IPAD I use for work, however the IPAD said the pictures were unavailable. After messing with it for hours trying to get the photos off of the IPAD, the IPAD randomly deleted all the images and synced with the ICloud account. I spent an hour on the phone with tech support and they couldn't help me retrieve them. Thankfully while fiddling around before they disappeared, I at least tried to send the photos to myself off the IPAD by using a "copy share link" and emailing all the links to myself. The photos never uploaded from the IPAD but I was left with these low-resolution cropped photo previews without dates or locations. I then had to print screen and paste them into new files.

These photos were taken in Tahoe Vista/Carnelian Bay August 2019 and the area has since undergone a massive forest fuels reduction treatment. The whole area is nothing but a few spread out standing trees and wood chips. It previously was a fairly normal forest habitat. You can even clearly see the full masticated area in the satellite image when you zoom in on this website down to "500m" scale shown at the bottom.
The 3rd to last picture you can see the drops of red staining along the stick going up and to the left in the picture.
The 2nd to last picture shows a stick with the red staining in a bush. I think I lifted the stick into the bush to take the picture and this is the stick I brought home with me and have since lost in my yard. I honestly can't remember if I found the stick in the bush like that or not but pretty sure I did.
The 4th to last picture shows it on a stick under a bush and rock in the lower right. This might be the same stick. I can't tell from these low quality and cropped images.
I have one other option to try to recover the images but it might take a couple days.
The last picture is a higher resolution image I was able to recover. You can see to spots on the bitterbrush and a stick on the ground.

It's a mystery!

description:
DSF
Beautiful in their arrangement, this flood of tiny pale, glossy eggs, was about 2ft up, on a young city-planted Beech(?) tree. At dusk they appear greyish. Days later, the mass seems more connected to each other as a form-fitting sheet, than stuck to the actual flexible leaf, due to a slight shadow under the edge. I didn’t curl the leaf down however, to find out. 
When taking the photo at dusk, I noticed a nearby small brown moth (with a broad horizontal-stripe design) fly west toward sunset at about 2ft and descending. Perhaps avoiding the autofocus. This array of eggs is 3-4 x larger than its full wingspan. 
I have no idea how just one insect could lay all these eggs. (Could they expand in air?)

In spring this tree had a lot of aphids being ‘farmed’ by tiny ants; (and a lot of fluffy-waxy-aphid-waste residue). No evidence remains. 
Maybe it’s from a Rusty Tussock Moth, but, also:
Perhaps it’s a stink bug that lures ants to care for it’s eggs and young. That would be fair turnaround! 
Perhaps aphids, or tree, receive something from stink-bugs? That would be so cool!  

I didn’t check for awhile, but by Oct 3 there are zero eggs left. Just a gluey-grid that kinda looks like rain smooshed some remaining edges together. I’m guessing the other grids slid off. Wondering if ants carried the eggs away to overwinter together?
I’m thinking that the grid-glue could be like egg-white protein, and when rain softened it, the eggs could easily slide off the leaf into the grass below. Ants would find the mass quickly, the glue-grid remaining on the leaf might be edible, some has curled at the lower edge.  I suppose birds could eat the eggs too, or save them for young to eat in spring.

The last ones get loose. They grow  on rows on septate hyphae. The fruitbody looks like a plume. Simple spores around 1.9 x 4.9 um. The other type are around 4.4um in high. Seems to belong to Moliniales but the family is not in inaturalist. Margarinomyces seems close to it.

description:
Possibly. Interior gelatinous, very sticky. Spores light brown, smooth walled. Growing in leaf litter, cypress, white oak, holly, beech, sourwood, tupelo, magnolia.  White rhizomorphs, fuzzy ball shaped exterior. 

Notes and last 6 photos by Django Grootmeyers:
Collected with, and found by, Alisha Millican. Growing scattered in leaf litter near Taxodium distichum, Quercus alba, Fagus grandifolia, Oxydendron arboreum, Nyssa sylvatica, Magnolia sp. and Ilex opaca. Basidiocarps reddish yellow (7.5YR 7/6 in Munsell); with fuzzy peridium; fragile and collapsing easily; attached by short stems to white to pale orange rhizomorphs; up to 18.1 mm wide. Gleba gelatinous. Lacking a clearly delimited columella. Odor not distinctive. Monomitic with simple-septate generative hyphae. Subhymenial hyphae gelatinized. Cystidia absent. Basidia 4-sterigmate. NUMBER: 20220911
SPECIES: Peach-Colored Fly Agaric, Amanita persicina (Jenkins, 1977)
OTHER NAMES: Formerly considered a subspecies or variety of the famous Fly Agaric, A. muscaria (Linnaeus, 1753).  All these names remain in use and controversial.  Possibly a morphological species, which had been allowed in mycology for hundreds of years.
DISTINCTIONS: Upper cap 4-20 cm (1.6-7.8 in) wide, color dull reddish-orange adorned with numerous yellowish cottony warts, lower white; stem 8-25 cm (3.1-9.8 in) long, 1-3 cm (0.4-1.2 in) thick, usually tapering to apex and flaring to an enlarged basal bulb, white, ring composed of a few fragments or often none.
DATE, TIME: 11 September 2022, 12:07 PM
LOCALITY: Urban Estates, Vineyards, Florida
LATITUDE, LONGITUDE: 26.20674, 81.73381
DISTRIBUTION: Eastern USA, mostly Southeastern, Texas to Georgia, with records in New Jersey and New York.  Pinterest (2022) noted Amanita persicina in north Florida, but not in central or south Florida.  iNaturalist (unpublished) did not list this mushroom in south Florida.  Our record represents a range extension into south Florida.
USE and DANGER: Has a pleasant taste and odor and is both psychoactive and poisonous (if not properly prepared by parboiling).  This statement above should not be considered a recommendation concerning edibility or safety.  This is a dangerous mushroom for consumption (Mcarthy et al., 2022).
ECOLOGY: Mycorrhizal (symbiotic with tiny roots) with trees.  This one was near the base of a Southern Live Oak Tree, Quercus virginiana Miller, 1768.

description:
Deer rub, White-Tailed Deer (Odocoileus virginianus) 
1.	Documentation: Tree indicates deer rub. This is common for this time of year from bucks. This area is also known for having a high deer population so I found this on multiple trees. The rub can also indicate what size the buck was. The diameter of the rub on the tree is somewhere between 4-6 inches, so I would assume this is a mature buck
2.	Scat: pellet like clumps found in the general area 
3.	Weather: cloudy, windy 
Temp: High: 51, Low: 32 
Precipitation: 0.00 in the last 24 hours
Wind:  12 mph 
Humidity: 46% 
4.	Nearby plants and Animals: Also found tracks of Common Raccoon (Procyon lotor), evidence of meadow vole (microtus pennsylvanicus), and a sighting of Virginia Opossum (didelphis virginiana) 
5.	Additional Notes: White-tailed deer are known for being in this area, I have seen multiple and have found previous evidence (tracks, scat, flattened beds in snow). A sign of them is deer rub, males rub bark off of trees with their antlers. They do this to mark their territory, show dominance, and intimidate other bucks, and it intensifies at the end of winter to help them shed their antlers. This also coincides with mating season so they will do this around September to February.  While doing this it rubs the bark off of the tree, marking where they did it.

description:
on Ulmus americana (or possibly alata). They grow at the base of the buds and only on one side of the twig, the lower "brown" side (the upper side is more gray). Typically one "body" per bud. I've been seeing these for 18 years, just like this. 

When wet, they plump up (see last photos for dry shots). 

Here's the first observation I made in 2005: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/106470935

Here's my entry at bugguide: https://bugguide.net/node/view/2088360

I'm not sure the white watery blobs (photos 4 and 7) are related. I found a few of them on the tree itself when rain had just stopped. I closely examined many twigs on the tree two days in a row, one rainy and the next sunny. I've found some of the "bodies" on one of the trees itself but so far they are smaller than the ones I've been finding on the ground underneath the tree. 

I've been through the scales here and don't think I've found any matches: http://scalenet.info/associates/Ulmus%20americana/

Here's a definite scale from the same tree: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/151059428

This is one of the elms I'm finding them under: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/151217612

I did an experiment with a "plumped" one I found on wet ground after a rain. I brought it home and several hours later it was dried out and "deflated". I put it in a small bowl of water and checked it in 15 minutes to find that it had rehydrated again. See last 3 photos. 

I added a set for smaller ones found on a tree (not on the ground): https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/151839406

Mar 23: After a rain, I noticed quite a few of them forming ascocarp trype structure. 5 photos added.

description:
At least 5 fungus bodies were seen on 30 June 2023, occurring along a 3 metre section on the north edge of Dune Track at Langwarrin Flora and Fauna Reserve, Victoria. Fungal bodies were between 15 and 20mm high. The soil was pale sand with very short moss. Associated plants include Allocasuarina sp., Leptospermum myrsinoides, Epacris impressa, Drosera peltata, Lepidosperma sieberi, and occasional stunted Eucalyptus viminalis.

The bodies closely resemble photo 300b, Aphelaria sp., in the book "A Field Guide to Australian Fungi" by Bruce Fuhrer, published in 2005 by Bloomings Books, Melbourne. The habitat given in that book is "... In wet eucalypt and pine forest ..." whereas they were seen in heathland.

Here are photos of a nearby cluster that looked like the same species: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/176530119

Photo 11 was brightened. Photos 12-14 were edited to have a Flash White Balance in Photoshop. Photo 15 was brightened and had lowered highlights to better show the ruler.

description: alguna sugerencia

While traveling through Fort Ord National Monument (14,651 acres)  today, we saw several dozen of these white, long, silky spider webs sailing through the air on the warm, gentle breeze. Some were tangled up in tall grasses or Telegraphweed. There were no spiders observed in any of these webs that we could find. Some of these strands were 50-60 ft long. Individual strands were very thin and sticky to the touch. Fascinating phenomenon!

Field Guide to Spiders of California and the Pacific Coast States, RJ Adams and Tim Manolis, 2014. Spider Webs and Silk pp. 11-14.

It may, or may not have been this:
“Spider Ballooning. Can Spiders Fly?
Spiders may not possess wings like birds, but they can easily fly hundreds to thousands of miles on strands of spider silk. The process, commonly called ballooning, allows spiders to become airborne by getting exposed to air currents and the Earth’s electric field. Although the ballooning behavior is typically displayed by the spiderlings to disperse, the adults are also observed doing so. Adult female velvet spiders, weighing over 100 mg, and having a size of about 14 mm have been spotted ballooning using rising air currents.

How do Spiders Fly

These eight-legged invertebrates use this airborne dispersal mechanism to move between different locations. A spiderling or an adult spider generally climbs up on a higher position, stands with its legs raised and abdomen pointed upward, and releases several threads of silk into the air. These threads form a triangle-shaped parachute, which helps the spider get dispersed away with the slightest of breezes. Scientists have found that the Earth’s electric field also helps the spiders fly in windless conditions.
Interesting Facts: In Australia, mass spider balloonings were reported in 2012 and 2015, during which the ground seemed snow-covered with the silk from millions of spiders that landed there.
Ballooning spiders are usually harmless because the venom of most spiderlings is not harmful.” https://spideridentifications.com/spider-facts/spider-ballooning

description:
This has been an interesting learning curve for me. Bought on by me always being curious. Plus some mistaken thinking. Although, I have photographed little wasps on this Ootheca over the last few months, I didn’t relate the tiny holes in the Ootheca to them. Instead I thought it meant the baby Praying Mantis had emerged out of them.
So, thinking it was old and empty, I wanted to see what it looked like on the inside. I was not prepared for what I found.

Inside I found the larvae of Genus Podagrion. The first two images are clearly female showing the unmistakable Ovipositor. As for the other images I’m not sure if some are just shedded skins. Not having a microscope I couldn’t tell. I put the Ootheca back together as best I could.The next morning I had one wasp.
Over the next few days 3 more hatched. All have been released now. I also learned that the little holes in the  Ootheca, are made by the female’s Ovipositor piercing through the Ootheca to deposit her eggs, onto the Mantis eggs, for them to feed on.

Habitat: On mossy mudbank (see photo 5), in this collection, the fruitbodies were attached to mud at least not apparently/directly attached to moss filaments. Macro Summary: Fruitbody 2-4mm (see photo 6), sessile, spathulate, flabelliform, some like mini ladles/scoops (see photo 4), margin wavy/undulate in largest specimens and when dry, white/cream, flesh thin translucent when fresh, more stereoid-looking when dry. Upper sterile surface finely felty under lens (also see photo 2 and 7). Hymenophore nearly smooth, barely any folds/wrinkles, translucent (see photos 1 and 3). Micro Summary: Microscopy was a bit of a bust. I wasn’t able to find spores either in sections or via spore print. These may be immature fruitbodies. description:
In bog

Lichen species provide **housing/shelter**, **symbiotic** within the lichen, & **construction**, wildlife & human

• **housing/shelter lichens**: lichens, a symbiotic partnership between fungi and algae/cyanobacteria; the algae/cyanobacteria provide food, the fungus **structural shelter** for algae/cyanobacteria, *etc*., also provide crucial **ecological shelter**, acting as habitats for invertebrates, and nesting materials for birds:

**Symbiosis** – **structural shelter**
◦ a basidiomycete fungus (a core partner yeast in the primary fungal partner's outer cortex, the 'skin') inaturalist.org/observations/301610979
◦ microbiome bacteria: (Proteobacteria), providing vitamins, growth hormones, & pathogen resistance  inaturalist.org/observations/301610979
◦ protists, kingdom Protista, on/in a lichen's microbiome (its entire community of microorganisms) inaturalist.org/observations/301610979
◦ bacteriophages (viruses infecting bacteria in bacterial communities within lichens; viruses also live in cytoplasm of hyphae in the lichen fungal partner (mycobiont) inaturalist.org/observations/301610979

**Construction** – **ecological shelter**
◦ invertebrate shelter: caterpillars, *e*.*g*., Psychidae family (Bagworm Moths), create protective, camouflaged bags using silk and specific lichens for shelter inaturalist.org/observations/226339273; Lichen-carrying Green Lacewing (*Leucochrysa pavida*) larvae inaturalist.org/observations/197251655
◦ wildlife habitat: lichens provide, or are found on, surfaces (like snags/dead wood) that offer food for small animals, birds, and insects; & shelter/nesting material inaturalist.org/observations/303710295
◦ artistic/functional usage: projects explore using lichens as artificial ("trans-species") wildlife housing

**– ...and also, "Coming Soon", even to a planet near you... -**

◦ artistic/functional usage: projects for people, like completely autonomous self-growing technology for expeditions to Mars developed by designing a synthetic community from multiple lichen species [stories.tamu.edu/news/2025/06/24/growing-homes-on-mars-texas-am-research-pioneers-autonomous-construction-using-synthetic-lichens/]

description:
HRL3297

Date de récolte : 14 septembre 2020
Localité : Chibougamau
Habitat : Terril, près de peuplier baumier et saule 
Substrat : Sable et petites roches, dans la mousse
Mode de croissance : Isolée à grégaire

DESCRIPTION

Pileus de 4-12,5 mm de largeur, plano-convexe, déprimé au centre, devenant étalé et déprimé, hygrophane, strié par transparence, brun grisâtre (7D3, 7E3, 6F4) à l’état imbu, gris orangé à orange grisâtre (5B2, 5B3) au sec, glabre.

Lames décurrentes, espacées, concolores au chapeau, environ 1,5 mm de largeur

Stipe 12-26 x 0,75-1,5 mm, égal, luisant, glabre, brun foncé (7F4), parfois torsadé.

Odeur et saveur fortement farino-cucumiques.

Contexte concolore, très mince. 

Spores 5-7(8) x 3-3,5 µm, moy. 5,9 x 3,1 µm, Q = 1,67-2,33, Q moyen = 1,91 µm, oblongues à cylindriques

Basides: 22-26 x 5,5-6 µm, tétrasporiques, bouclées. 

Hyphes de la trame lamellaire bouclées.

Les spores sont un peu plus étroites que dans la description d'Arnolds, ce qui donne un Q un peu plus élevé. Outre cette différence, il n'existe aucune différence marquée avec l'espèce européenne. La forte odeur farino-cucumique est distinctive. Aucune séquence d'Omphalina microsperma n'est disponible dans les bases de données. 

Réf. 
Arnolds, Eif. 1982. Ecology and coenology of macrofungi in grasslands and moist heathlands in Drenthe, the Netherlands. Vol. 2. Bibliotheca Mycologica 90.

Bon, M., Moreau, P-A. 1998. Une omphale microspore et farinolente (Omphalina baeospora var. microsperma (Arnolds) stat. nov. Documents mycologiques 23(111):69-70.

So they are a little tiny rectangles uniformly 3 mm wide by 5 mm long and approximately 2 mm high. At first glance they appear caterpillar but lack the grooves. It not match anything we see of similar size like Merriam's kangaroo scat, bat guano or Peromyscus.    Is there any caterpillar scat that can appear without the longitudinal grooves? description:
Location: Pskem River bank, Western Tian Shan, Uzbekistan.
Date: March 28, 2026.
​Observation Details:
During the field survey, I documented several large tracks along the riverbank in wet mud and hard soil. The primary focus of this observation is a series of tracks consistent with the Striped Hyena (Hyaena hyaena).
​Key Morphological Features:
​Claw Marks: Distinct, thick, and blunt claw impressions are clearly visible at the tip of each toe pad. This is a diagnostic feature for hyaenids, distinguishing them from large felids which usually retract claws during normal gait.
​Size: The tracks measure approximately 12.5 cm to 13 cm in length (including claws).
​Track Asymmetry: The forefoot tracks are significantly larger and broader than the hindfoot, reflecting the heavy-set front anatomy of the species.
​Pad Structure: The interdigital space and the shape of the plantar pad suggest a non-felid structure, specifically aligning with Hyaena hyaena morphology.
​Context:
The tracks were found in a corridor characterized by high predator-scavenger activity. Nearby, unidentified large felid tracks (~13x10 cm, no claws) and territorial scrapings were also noted. This indicates a complex predator interaction dynamic in the Pskem valley.
